scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Batuque is widely regarded as the oldest musical and dance tradition in Cape Verde.

While musicologist Carlos Gonçalves notes it is not simply an unmediated African import but rather an adaptation of African dance forms that evolved distinct local features in Cape Verde, written records trace it back to the 18th century.
The earliest documented colonial decree against it was signed in September 1772 by Governor Joaquim Salema de Saldanha Lobo, citing nighttime disruptions and scandalous gatherings.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: In earlier centuries, batuque held specific social, ritual, and ceremonial importance.
It was danced on Christian saints' feast days, at local festivals, and especially prior to and during weddings.
Scholars have suggested that the pelvic movements originally evoked fertility and marital sexuality to bless the bride.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: A batuque dance takes place within an open circle called a terreru, situated in an outdoor patio or town square.
Women form the circle, acting as musicians and chorus.
When the first musical movement (galion) begins, a solo dancer ties a cloth sash (panu) around her hips and moves into the center.
Watch for galion movement, da ku tornu.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Musically, batuque is characterized by an andante tempo set in 6/8 or 3/4 meter and defined by call-and-response vocal structures.
It is Cape Verde's only native polyrhythmic tradition, overlaying a 3-beat rhythm across a 2-beat pulse.
Listen for the Cloths slapped between thighs (pano), Hand clapping, Cimboa (extinct / historical).
The pulse is 6/8 or 3/4.

A dense, driving acoustic texture characterized by bare hands slapping folded cloths held between thighs in an insistent three-over-two polyrhythm. A solo female voice delivers poetic, improvised lines that are answered by a full-throated unison female chorus, building gradually from an andante dialogue into a rapid, thumping percussive climax.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Batuque requires no specialized architecture and takes place in a terreru, typically an open-air domestic backyard or a public village square.
Dancers wear everyday attire accented by a panu—a traditional fabric cloth tied securely around the waist or hips to visually accentuate the oscillatory movements of the pelvis.
The seated or crouching batukaderas place folded cloths firmly between their thighs, turning everyday textiles into percussive striking surfaces.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historic and modern practitioners include singer Nácia Gomes, whose lyrics highlighted the hardships of rural life, and the late composer Orlando Pantera, who led the genre's artistic revival in the 1990s alongside composers Tcheka and Vadú.
Contemporary vocalists such as Lura, Mayra Andrade, and Nancy Vieira popularized batuque internationally.
While historical evidence suggests batuque was once widespread across all Cape Verdean islands, it survived into modern times almost exclusively on the island of Santiago.
Batuque developed as a Creole adaptation of continental African dances during the early colonial settlement of the Cape Verde archipelago.

scenes.title: Try one step
narration: Before we go, one step. Stand in the center of the terreru with a panu tied around the hips.
Execute the galion phase by swaying the body gently while shifting weight between alternate legs on the downbeat.
Count it: 1-2-3, 4-5-6 (six subdivisions grouped in two; practice pulse only).
